rows.title: Nuclear Atlas — Why it exists
rows.summary: A developer wants to ask about the project in front of them and to hand small work to an agent, without the code leaving the machine and without paying a frontier model for every token.
body: A developer wants to ask about the project in front of them and to hand small work to an agent, without the code leaving the machine and without paying a
frontier model for every token. Nuclear Atlas sends a question to the local assistant of the
[Nuclear Developer](../../../nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/README.md) with the project's map
(`.nuclear/map.md`, written by the build) and the last messages of the session; the assistant answers from that map
and the [Smart Graph](../../../nuclear-graph-storage/README.md). An order runs as a
[Nuclear Builder](../nuclear-builder/README.md) run by the local agents: plan, tests first, code, tests, security
review; its journal is the answer.
What it leaves out: Nuclear Atlas never calls a model by itself (questions go to the Developer, orders to the Builder),
and it is VS Code only.

body: A message goes to `POST /developer/chat` of the Nuclear Developer with:

rows.title: Nuclear Builder — Why it exists
rows.summary: Work with AI agents should start from a spec and end in tested, reviewed code, with every step visible, and the same pipeline should run on a server.
body: Work with AI agents should start from a spec and end in tested, reviewed code, with every step visible, and the same
pipeline should run on a server. A frontier model that does everything is paid for every token and the code leaves
the machine; a local 3B model alone cannot hold a whole feature. The Builder puts them in the roles of a lead and a
junior: Claude makes the decisions (the plan, the names, the review), the local Nuclear Developer writes each piece,
and what the junior cannot fix the lead fixes and keeps as an example.
What it leaves out on purpose: the shell runs nothing that is not in `.nuclear/builder.json`; the agent stages do
not run on a server (the server checks their result with the deterministic stages); the acceptance step informs and
never fails a run; there is no Builder for Zed.

rows.title: Domain: spec, run, stage, step, actor — How the work is split
rows.summary: So that the local 3B models only think the business logic: 1. Before anyone writes, the transpiler has written the project map.
body: So that the local 3B models only think the business logic:
1. Before anyone writes, the transpiler has written the **project map**. The agents read it instead of every file,
so each declaration should have a one-line description (its `//` doc comment).
2. **Tests first**: the tester writes one test per acceptance criterion, with the names the plan gives.

3. **Code**: the coder writes each piece at its place (`nuclear help layout --platform

`), with the card of its
kind, the mistakes to avoid with that kind, examples of it and the project's files that declare the names its
task writes (it reads them by itself). The compiler checks it, then the whole project.
4. **Verification**: every test runs. A failing test goes back to the coder told in Nuclear (`nuclear explain`:
the message, a hint and the `.nuc` lines), up to three rounds; when Claude leads, it fixes what is left.

rows.title: Domain: spec, run, stage, step, actor — Invariants
rows.summary: Invariants
body: - The local agents only ever see Nuclear and the platform (backend, mobile, web), never Python, TypeScript or Dart.
- A spec needs at least one acceptance criterion.
- Nothing is guessed: a request that lacks a fact its strategy needs stops at the analysis, with the question.
- A bug's repair goes to the file the failure names, whoever wrote it, and never to the test.
- Two processes never run the same run.
- A file the user changed since the run wrote it is never undone.

rows.title: The engine (`engine.ts`, `safety.ts`) — What keeps a run safe (`safety.ts`, ADR-platform-0003)
rows.summary: `STALE_MS` (45 s) means its owner stopped.
body: - `atomicWrite`: the run's state is never half written.
- `trace` / `readTrace`: every event, as JSON lines, append-only.
- `owner` / `alive` / `orphaned`: the process that runs a run beats every `BEAT_MS` (10 s); a heartbeat older than
`STALE_MS` (45 s) means its owner stopped.
- The ledger (`Run.writes`): every file the run writes, with what was there before (`writeFile` keeps it);
`rollback` undoes it.
- `checkConnections`: the services, the models, the tools' `--version`, `freeMb`. `ollamaBusy` (`/api/ps`).
In the engine:
- `start` refuses a run another live process owns, recovers an orphaned one, beats, and runs `preflight` (*Check the
connections*: the Developer, the graph, Ollama and the models, Claude when it leads, free disk) before the first
stage it runs.
- `watched` cuts a call (`StallError`) after `callTimeoutMs` (15 minutes by default), or after `stallSeconds` (90)
with neither the Developer nor a model working on it; the call is retried.
- A command gets `commandTimeoutMs` (20 minutes): `TIMED_OUT`, and its process group is killed.
- `recoverRun` / `recoverRuns`: what an interrupted run left half written is undone, and it goes on from that step.
In VS Code, `resumeOrphans` does it on activation (`nuclear.ai.resumeInterrupted`), with a notification.

rows.title: Follow a run — The strategy of a request
rows.summary: What a strategy changes in a run: first (`nuclear fix .`), then each file with errors is repaired with the card of each error.
body: What a strategy changes in a run:
- **The stages that run.** A compile error skips *Generate*, *Plan* and *Tests first*: the compiler's exact fixes
first (`nuclear fix .`), then each file with errors is repaired with the card of each error. A failing test goes
straight to *Verification*. A rename plans and writes, and writes no test.
- **Where the pieces come from.** For a new feature the planner splits what the generators left. For a change of
something that exists (a field more, a column) the pieces are the files that declare it. For a rename a tool
gives every file that writes the name, already rewritten: no model writes.
- **What is asked first.** A stored resource without its fields, a rename without its two names, a bug without what
should happen: the analysis stops the run with the question. Nothing is guessed.
- **The wiring.** After *Code*, each use case the coder wrote is wired by `nuclear gen usecase`: its alias in the
facade and, when the spec's sentence gives it (`POST orders/{id}/cancel`), its route.
- **A bug's repair** goes to the file the failure names, whoever wrote it, and never to the test.
A request that is not a run (a question, a command, something beyond the platform) stops at the analysis and says
where it belongs. When the analysis read it wrong, name the strategy in the spec (`- Strategy: usecase`, under
`- Use case:`) and run it again.

for each kind of request (31 rows, `strategy:<name>`; ADR-developer-0001): how the kind is recognised, its plan with the
tool of every step, and what it asks of a run. The local **analyst** picks it before anything is generated or
planned. No model chooses: the request's exact signs decide (a diagnostic code, a test's output, `rename A to B`, a
`GET <url>` line), then its meaning, and whether the project already has the names it writes.
| Family | Kinds of request |
| create | a whole system, a project, a component, a resource of another API, a stored resource, the app of a backend, only an interface, a repository, a use case, a route, one declaration |
| change | one more field, method or action; a rename; a move or an extraction; a break of the architecture's rules; the database's schema; the configuration; taking something out |
| fix | it does not compile; a test fails; it does the wrong thing; it fails while running; the data does not match; a screen shows the wrong thing; the machine or a service fails |
| verify and explain | tests for what exists; a security review; documentation; a question; building, running and shipping |
| beyond | what NuclearLang or the local agents cannot do: said before anything is written |

rows.title: Nuclear Developer — Why it exists
rows.summary: A frontier model that does all the work of a spec is paid for every token, and the code leaves the machine.
body: A frontier model that does all the work of a spec is paid for every token, and the code leaves the machine. A model
small enough for a developer's laptop cannot hold much context, chooses tools badly, and the machine has no GPU to
train one. So the work is split as a lead splits it with a junior: the lead (Claude, or you) makes the decisions
(the plan, the names, the review) and the local developer writes each piece. What the junior cannot fix, the lead
fixes and keeps as an example in the graph, so the junior gets it right next time.
What it leaves out: the agents write only Nuclear, for a platform (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`), never a dialect or
a target language; and a model writes nothing a tool can write.

rows.title: Vision — Problem
rows.summary: A frontier model that does all the work of a spec is paid for every token, and the code leaves the machine.
body: A frontier model that does all the work of a spec is paid for every token, and the code leaves the machine. A model
small enough to run on a developer's laptop (at most 3B parameters) cannot hold much context, chooses tools badly,
and the machine has no GPU to train one.
The Nuclear Developer is a set of local agents for NuclearLang and Synapsis that work as **the junior developer of
a frontier model**: a lead (Claude, or the user) makes the decisions (the plan, the names, the review) and the
local developer writes each piece. What a small model cannot hold in its head comes from the
[Nuclear Smart Graph](../../../../nuclear-graph-storage/README.md); what it writes is checked by the Nuclear
compiler before it answers. What the junior cannot fix, the lead fixes and keeps as an example in the graph, so the
junior gets it right next time.

rows.title: Vision — The idea behind the design
rows.summary: (recall, write, check, repair), never a model with a toolbox.
body: - **A small model follows fixed steps better than it chooses tools.** Each agent is a graph with fixed steps
(recall, write, check, repair), never a model with a toolbox.
- **Tools before models.** A generator writes what is standard, the compiler's exact fixes come before any repair,
a rename is done by a tool: a model writes only a piece of one file that no tool can write.
- **The agents are trained by retrieval and distillation**, not by changing weights: a failure is fixed with a
general rule or more knowledge in the graph, never with the answer.

rows.title: Vision — What it does not do
rows.summary: `web`), never a dialect.
body: - It does not choose names, data or architecture: the order gives them.
- It does not write a target language. The agents write only Nuclear: they name a platform (`backend`, `mobile`,
`web`), never a dialect.
- It does not run a model larger than 3B parameters of effective size (the user's rule).
- Its assistant does not change a file: an order is a run of the Builder.
- It does not hide what is beyond it: the plan and the analysis say so before anything is written
([the limits](../02-architecture/overview.md#known-limits)).

- **Nuclear Atlas** of the editor: a question about the project, or an order.

rows.title: Integrations and contracts — The HTTP API
body: On `127.0.0.1:7879`. Every route is `POST /developer/<name>` and answers `200`.
| Route | Request | Answer |
| `code`, `test`, `security` | `{task, platform = "backend", path, kind, context, root}` | `{code, report, check, attempts, trace: [{step, detail}]}` |
| `document` | the same; the run's journal in `context` | the same; the summary in `report` |
| `diagnose` | the same; `task` is the step, `context` its output, `path` the project's folder | the same |
| `accept` | the same; `task` the criteria, numbered; `context` the facts and the files of the run | the same |
| `chat` | `{message, platform, map, history, root}` | the same answer (`report`) |
| `plan` | `{spec, platform, root}` | `{pieces: [{path, kind, task}], raw, trace, tree, limits}` |
| `analyze` | `{spec, platform, root, strategy}` | `{strategy, title, why, mode, stages, lead, source, generate, pieces, questions, limits, report, trace}` |
- `platform` is `backend`, `mobile` or `web`: the agents name a platform, never a dialect.
- `root` is the project's folder: with it an agent reads the project by itself.
- `trace` is the steps the agent followed, with what it read.

rows.summary: The Builder, Nuclear Atlas and `nuclear-builder` are the project `extensions/`; the MCP tools (`developer_task`, `developer_retry`, `developer_review`, `developer_code`, `developer_test`, `developer_security`) are the project `tools/mcp`.
body: The Builder, Nuclear Atlas and `nuclear-builder` are the project [`extensions/`](../../../../extensions/AGENTS.md); the MCP
tools (`developer_task`, `developer_retry`, `developer_review`, `developer_code`, `developer_test`,
`developer_security`) are the project [`tools/mcp`](../../../../tools/mcp/AGENTS.md).
**Every run is documented.** `.nuclear/builder/runs/<id>.md` (beside the `.json` with every log whole): the
documenter's summary (what it built, how it checked it, what is left), why it failed (the diagnoser), the files
written, what is left for the reviewer, and each step with its agent, its trace and what it read; a frontier
model's review is `<id>.review.md`.
**When something fails.** A call to the Developer that fails for a passing reason (down, busy, 408/425/429/5xx) is
retried by its caller with exponential backoff and full jitter (5 tries, 1–30 s by default; `Retry-After` wins). A
compiler error or a failing test is never retried blindly: it goes to the repair rounds, then to the diagnoser
(kind by rules: transient, environment, code, test, spec; evidence from `nuclear check` or `nuclear doctor`; the
next step). A failed run goes on from the step that failed (*↻ Retry*, `nuclear-builder retry <run>`,
`developer_retry`): every step that passed is kept, the earlier attempt stays in the run file.

rows.summary: model got a test of an application component from the examples): the run fails at *Tests first* with the diagnosis instead of passing without tests; Claude-led runs fix it.
body: - The 3B tester copies a solved example of the graph when it is close to the task (a spec that declares only a
model got a test of an application component from the examples): the run fails at *Tests first* with the
diagnosis instead of passing without tests; Claude-led runs fix it.
- The planner maps a kind only from its own word ("application component" is not `appcomponent`) and names a
component after the first model of a plain spec (`newbooks`).
- A value that comes from a library method has no known type: declare it (`card: string = ~knowledge.card(...)`)
before using a member of the standard library on it.
- The connections set no limit on the length of an answer (`config/project_config.nuc` gives the context window
only): a model that enters an answer without end holds the Developer and every call after it until the process
is killed. Seen with `qwen2.5-coder:3b` as assistant, `llama3.2:1b` and `phi3:3.8b`; the evaluation has no watch
on a call that stalls.
- On features of several files written by the local agents alone, a piece renames a method the spec writes, or two
pieces declare the same thing. That is why a feature goes through the generators first and, when it has a design
of its own, under a lead.

| Who | Asks the graph for |
| The coder | `kind:<platform>.<kind>` by its id, the pitfalls whose `kinds` list has that kind, solved tasks and an example file of that kind |
| A repair | `error:<code>` of each code the compiler named |
| The assistant | every shelf with the question, each card with the rows it links to; and the exact facts of a question with one right answer |
| The diagnoser | the cards of the codes in a log and the closest known failures |
**What the agents may read.** Only Nuclear and the platform (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`): a row the agents read
has no target-language code (the build of the knowledge base refuses one that has), a failing test reaches them
told in `.nuc` terms, a piece's errors are given by line, and the diagnoser's prompt forbids speaking of the
generated code. They check with `nuclear check --platform`.
**What it knows** is the knowledge base of the Smart Graph
([`nuclear-graph-storage/data`](../../../../nuclear-graph-storage/data/README.md)); the agents read every row but
the ones about the target languages and the dialects underneath (`agents: false`).

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — Limits
rows.summary: (the platform binds a repository to its entity by its name, so an entity renamed alone compiles and fails when it runs).
body: - `refactor-move-extract`, `remove` and `beyond` need a lead: the local agents do their mechanical steps only.
- A rename by the tool covers a declaration's name and the declarations built from it by a word before or after
(the platform binds a repository to its entity by its name, so an entity renamed alone compiles and fails when
it runs). That also takes a declaration that only starts with the name (`OrderLine` with `Order`): the analysis
lists every name it changes. A field or a method is renamed by hand (the same word may be another declaration's
member); the file of a renamed declaration keeps its path; a plural (`ListBooks`) and an alias of the facade
stay. A rename runs no security review: it writes no new logic.
- A bug whose failure names only its test stops at *Verification*: where the cause is needs a lead or the user.
- The Builder writes files and never deletes one.
- Still by hand or by a model, with no generator: relations in a stored resource, the tests of a backend resource
over another API, what a screen shows of a use case added with `gen usecase` (mobile, web).

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — The analyst
rows.summary: `components/developer/ai/analyst.nuc`, `POST /developer/analyze`.
body: `components/developer/ai/analyst.nuc`, `POST /developer/analyze`. It runs before anything is generated or planned,
in fixed steps:
1. The project's files say which names of the request exist.
2. The graph gives the strategy (by the request's exact signs, then its meaning, and by which of its names the
project has).
3. The strategy gives the stages that run, the source of the pieces and the facts it needs.
4. **A model is asked for one thing only**: the resources a request in plain words describes
(`component | Name | fields | source | actions`). Each line becomes a `nuclear gen resource` call and is kept
only if its `--dry-run` accepts it.
5. A fact the request lacks is a question for the user and stops the run: nothing is guessed.
It answers the strategy and why, the stages, the generator calls, the pieces the tools already gave (the files that
declare what changes; every file of a rename, rewritten) and the questions.
A model asked about a request that lists no field invents them. So it is asked only when the request lists some,
and its answer is held to that list: the number of fields must be the request's, it is asked once more when it is
not, and left out (the fields are then asked to the user) when the second answer fails too. Types it reads from
words (`total` as `double`) are shown in the *Generate* step of the run, to be checked there.

rows.summary: A whole system, one screen, a rename and a failing test are not done the same way.
body: A whole system, one screen, a rename and a failing test are not done the same way. The knowledge base holds a
**strategy** for each kind of request a user makes (31 rows, `strategy:<name>`, on the `playbooks` shelf of the
Smart Graph): how the kind is recognised, its plan step by step with the tool of every step, and what it asks of a
run. Changing how a kind of request is handled is changing a row, never code. Why: `ADR-developer-0001`.

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — Tools before models
rows.summary: In every strategy: `nuclear gen resource suppliers Supplier --fields "name:string phone:string" --source db --actions create,delete,update`, shown before it runs.
body: In every strategy:
- A generator writes what is standard. "Suppliers with a name and a phone: add, change and remove them" becomes
`nuclear gen resource suppliers Supplier --fields "name:string phone:string" --source db --actions
create,delete,update`, shown before it runs.
- The compiler's exact fixes (`nuclear fix`) come before any repair.
- A rename is done by a tool and no model writes (`Workspace.renamed`): every file that writes the name as a word,
with the new one in its place, and with it the project's names built from it (`NewBook` and `BookRepository` for
`Book`).
- The files a change starts in are found by the project's declarations, not planned.
- A generator finishes what it starts on a resource that exists: `nuclear gen resource` with a new action adds
the repository's method and the controller's route too (merged member by member). It refuses a search of a
stored resource, because which column is searched is a decision (a query of the repository, wired with
`nuclear gen usecase --calls`).
A model writes only a piece of one file that no tool can write.

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — What a run does with it
rows.summary: The Builder follows the strategy (the project `extensions/` has the pipeline): the analysis is the last step of the *Specification* stage; the stages the strategy has no use for are skipped; and asks the planner only when the strategy's pieces come from a plan; *Code* writes a piece a tool already…
body: The Builder follows the strategy (the project [`extensions/`](../../../../extensions/AGENTS.md) has the pipeline):
the analysis is the last step of the *Specification* stage; the stages the strategy has no use for are skipped;
*Generate* runs the spec's own resources and the calls the analysis derived; *Plan* takes the pieces the tools gave
and asks the planner only when the strategy's pieces come from a plan; *Code* writes a piece a tool already wrote
as it is, and afterwards wires each use case the coder wrote with `nuclear gen usecase` (its alias and, when the
spec's sentence gives it, its route); *Verification*, for a bug, repairs the file the failure names whoever wrote
it, and never the test. A Developer without an analyst leaves the run as it was: every stage. A lead model gets
the same routing and the same plans over MCP (`graph_strategy`).

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — What a strategy row says
rows.summary: Besides its card for people and lead models: Which strategy a request gets is chosen by the graph, without a model (the selection).
body: Besides its card for people and lead models:
| Field | Meaning |
| `data.signals` | regular expressions over the request: its exact signs (a diagnostic code, a test's output, `rename A to B`, a `GET <url>` line) |
| `meta.triggers` | the words that point to it |
| `data.target` | `existing`: the request names a declaration the project has; `new`: one it has not |
| `asks` | how people ask for it, in English and Spanish: found by meaning |
| `data.mode` | `write`, `repair` (the compiler's errors drive), `fix` (a failing test drives), `review`, `answer`, `commands`, `lead` |
| `data.stages` | the stages of the Builder it runs; empty: this kind of request is not a run |

| `data.pieces` | where its pieces come from: `plan` (the planner splits what is left), `declaring` (the files that declare what the request names), `naming` (every file that writes a name: a rename), `none` |
| `data.generators` | the generators it calls |
| `data.needs` | the facts it cannot start without, each with its question for the user |
| `data.lead` | `frontier` when it needs a model that understands several files at once |
Which strategy a request gets is chosen by the graph, without a model
([the selection](../../../../nuclear-graph-storage/docs/02-architecture/search.md#a-strategy)). A spec may name its
strategy itself (`- Strategy: usecase`).

rows.title: The Nuclear Developer
rows.summary: The Nuclear Developer is a team of small local agents (at most 3B parameters, on Ollama) that work as the junior developer of a frontier model.
body: The Nuclear Developer is a team of small local agents (at most 3B parameters, on Ollama) that work as **the junior
developer of a frontier model**. A lead (Claude, another frontier model, or you) makes the decisions: the plan, the
names, the review. The local agents write each piece. What a small model cannot hold in its head comes from the
[Smart Graph](../../../../nuclear-graph-storage/docs/08-guides/README.md); what it writes is checked by the Nuclear
compiler before it answers. Your code stays on your machine, and the lead spends tokens only on leading and
correcting.
**Tools before models.** A product is made with the platform's tools
([ADR-platform-0004](../../../../docs/03-adr/0004-products-are-made-with-the-tools.md)): `nuclear new`, `gen` and
`make` write what is standard, `nuclear fix` applies the compiler's exact fixes, a rename is done by a tool. The
Developer writes only what those leave, and only in Nuclear: it names a platform (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`),
never a dialect, and never writes target code.

rows.title: The Nuclear Developer — What a task goes through
rows.summary: A task (a spec) is a run of the Builder with the local agents: 1. Analysis.
body: A task (a spec) is a run of the Builder with the local agents:
1. **Analysis.** Which kind of request it is (a resource, a screen, a rename, a failing test...), which generator
calls cover it, and what the platform cannot do yet. It asks you when the request lacks a name or a field.
2. **Plan.** The planner splits the spec into pieces, one file each, and says what is beyond the agents (`limits`).
3. **Tests first.** The tester writes the Nuclear tests.
4. **Code.** The coder writes each piece, checks it with `nuclear check` and repairs it with the card of each error
(at most three attempts), and with the failing tests told in Nuclear (`nuclear explain`).
5. **Verification.** The project is checked and its tests run.
6. **Security.** The security reviewer reads each new file.
7. **Journal.** The documenter writes what was built, how it was checked and what is left. When a stage fails, the
diagnoser says why (transient, environment, code, test, spec) and what to do next.
Every run is written to `.nuclear/builder/runs/<id>.md` in the project, beside a `.json` with every log whole; a
lead's review is `<id>.review.md`.

rows.title: The Nuclear Developer — What it cannot do yet
rows.summary: From the roadmap: `gen resource --source db`, a search of a stored resource, a field added to a resource that exists, tests for a backend REST resource, what a screen shows of a use case.
body: From [the roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md):
- It does not choose names, data or architecture: the order gives them.
- Some requests still need a model or your hand because no tool covers them yet: relations in
`gen resource --source db`, a search of a stored resource, a field added to a resource that exists, tests for a
backend REST resource, what a screen shows of a use case. The Builder never deletes or moves a file, and a rename
covers declarations, not fields or methods.
- The security reviewer stops a backend run that changes data with a "missing authorization check" the platform
cannot express yet.
- A spec in plain words plans worse than one written with the platform's words (`use case`, `repository`...).
- The strategies ran end to end only on a `fastapi` project: never on a mobile or web project, never with
`nestjs`, never led by Claude.
- When a model enters an answer without end, every call waits: restart the Developer
([run it](../06-runbooks/run.md#when-it-fails)).

body: The private library of everything NuclearLang and Synapsis are, on the developer's machine (the RAG of the
platform): shelves of typed, linked, versioned cards, the exact facts of the base in a relational database, the
knowledge base those are made from (`data/`), and an HTTP server with access control. Agents (frontier models over
MCP, the local agents of the Nuclear Developer) ask it instead of guessing. ADR key: `graph`.
The platform's rules are the root [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md).

rows.title: Nuclear Smart Graph — Rules
rows.summary: `nuclear build .`, the tests.
body: - **It is written in Nuclear.** The `.nuc` files are the source. After a change: `nuclear check .`,
`nuclear build .`, the tests. What Nuclear cannot express is a finding of the compiler for the language's roadmap
(`../nuclearlang/docs/01-product/roadmap.md`), never a `.py` file written by hand.
- **Never weaken a security rule** (a token on every route, no `Origin`, encryption at rest, only ingest writes the
shelves of the base) to make something easier: build the access the right way (`connect`, a request the user
allows). The exact facts are never written to disk: the database is made in memory from the sealed cards
(`facts.nuc`).
- **The knowledge base is rows, not copied documents.** What has a structured source is generated (the
`extract_*.nuc` modules), never written by hand; what is written by hand names its sources. `shelves.nuc` is the
schema: a new shelf, type or filter is added there, with a test.
- **A question with one right answer** (which, how many, what are) is a row of `data/assets/queries/` over the
views of `facts.nuc`, never a card someone keeps in step by hand: a new kind of fact is a view, a new question a
row with its parameters, and an entry of `data/questions.toml` with `exact = true`.
- **After any change here or in the tree:** `nuclear-graph knowledge build`, `knowledge check`, `ingest`,

rows.title: Nuclear Smart Graph — Rules
rows.summary: `knowledge ask` (every question finds its row) and `knowledge examples` (every Nuclear example compiles).
body: `knowledge ask` (every question finds its row) and `knowledge examples` (every Nuclear example compiles).
- **The prompts in `prompts/` are measured** by the evaluation of the Nuclear Developer
(`../nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/eval`): a change is a new round, recorded in its report.
- A change to a route, to the client or to a setting updates `docs/02-architecture/integrations.md`. A structural
decision is a new ADR in `docs/03-adr/`. What cannot be read from the code or the documents is asked, not
invented.

rows.title: Nuclear Smart Graph — Stack
rows.summary: writes the Python package `build/nuclear_graph`, which `pyproject.toml` packages (Python 3.12+, uv, hatchling).
body: - **Source:** Nuclear, the `python` dialect (`*.nuc` at the root of this folder, `nuclear.toml`). `nuclear build .`
writes the Python package `build/nuclear_graph`, which `pyproject.toml` packages (Python 3.12+, uv, hatchling).
- **Store:** Chroma, one collection per shelf, documents encrypted (AES-256-GCM); vectors by `embeddinggemma` on
Ollama; the exact facts in SQLite, in memory only.
- **Server:** FastAPI + uvicorn on `127.0.0.1:7878`, a token on every route. The client (`nuclear_graph.client`)
needs only `httpx`.
- **The MCP server** is not here: it is the project [`tools/mcp`](../tools/mcp/AGENTS.md) (command `nuclear-mcp`),
which imports this package. `nuclear-graph mcp` runs `nuclear-mcp`; `knowledge build` reads its tools with
`nuclear-mcp tools`.

rows.title: Nuclear Smart Graph — Why it exists
rows.summary: An agent that writes Nuclear guesses what it does not know.
body: An agent that writes Nuclear guesses what it does not know. Cutting every markdown file of the tree into pieces does
not stop that: a piece knows its file and little else, and a search by meaning gives the closest pieces, never *all*
of something. Asked for every tool of the MCP server, it gives four and a model fills in the rest from memory.
The Smart Graph is a library of cards on shelves instead: each card answers one question and links to the cards it
has to do with. A question with one right answer (which, how many, what are) gets every row, the same on every run,
whatever the model.
What it is not, on purpose:
- **Not a copy of the documentation**, and not the teaching material nor the projects' pending work.
- **Not a model.** The search, the choice of a strategy and the query planner ask no model; only the embeddings are
computed.
- **Not shared.** It runs on the developer's machine for one OS user, and no program reads it until the user allows
it.

is for, what it can and cannot do, which tool does what, how a task is done or what an error has to do with another.
And a search by meaning gives the closest cards, never *all* of something: asked for every tool of the MCP server,
it gives four and a model fills in the rest from memory.
The Smart Graph is the local, private library of everything NuclearLang and Synapsis are. Agents ask it instead of
guessing: what Nuclear is for, how each thing is written, every kind and decorator, every tool, every error and its

body: A search by meaning gives the closest cards, never *all* of something: asked for every tool of the MCP server, it
gives four cards and a model fills in the rest. So the graph also holds **the exact facts** of the base in a
relational database, and a planner that answers from them without a model.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — How an answer reaches a person
rows.summary: The rows reach the reader as they are.
body: The rows reach the reader as they are. The assistant of the Nuclear Developer calls the planner before its model;
its prompt has an "Exact facts" section above the documentation, left out whole when no query ran. The model
explains the rows, and the rows themselves end the answer, put there by code: a list never depends on a model.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — The catalogue: the `queries` shelf
rows.summary: `data/assets/queries/exact.json`, a shelf like every other.
body: `data/assets/queries/exact.json`, a shelf like every other. A row is one question with one right answer
(`query:mcp.tools`, `query:mcp.group`, `query:kind.create`, `query:cli.commands`, `query:diagnostic`...):
- the ways people ask it, in English and Spanish;
- its parameters. Each names the query that lists *what people write* and *the value it means* (`generadores` →
`generate`, `caso de uso` → `usecase`, `generate resource` → `generate_resource`): no word list lives in code;
- its SQL, one `SELECT` over the views, and the heading of each column.
The build runs every query against empty tables and refuses a base whose query does not run, names a parameter it
does not declare, or declares one it never uses.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — The facts
rows.summary: `facts.nuc`.
body: `facts.nuc`. A SQLite database with the rows of the base without their bodies:
| Table | Holds |
| `cards` | id, shelf, type, title, summary |
| `platforms`, `keys`, `links` | a row's platforms, exact names and links |
| `fields`, `items` | every value of a row's `meta` and `data`, flattened |
| `about` | the revision |
One **view** per thing a question can list: `commands`, `mcp_tools`, `mcp_params`, `routes`, `kinds`, `kind_names`,
`decorators`, `plugins`, `dialects`, `generator_pieces`, `layout`, `diagnostics`, `habits`, `library`, `stages`,
`agents`, `components`, `editor_commands`, `editor_settings`, `strategies`, `capabilities`. The generated rows carry
what the views read as structured `data` (a tool's parameters, a command's usage, a generator's pieces).
**The database lives in memory only.** The store's rule is encryption at rest, and a SQLite file would keep names
and summaries in clear. The graph's process makes the database from the cards the store keeps sealed, at the first
question after it starts (a read of every card of the store, once) and again at every ingest, marks it read-only
(`PRAGMA query_only`) and writes nothing of it to disk. It holds no row's body and nothing an agent kept at run
time.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — The planner
rows.summary: It answers `facts` (the rows, whole, with their columns), `knowledge` (the cards) and `needs` (an exact question it is close to that lacks a name).
body: It answers `facts` (the rows, whole, with their columns), `knowledge` (the cards) and `needs` (an exact question it
is close to that lacks a name).

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — The planner
rows.summary: `planner.nuc`; `POST /v1/answer`, `nuclear-graph answer "<question>"`, MCP `graph_answer`.
body: `planner.nuc`; `POST /v1/answer`, `nuclear-graph answer "<question>"`, MCP `graph_answer`. It asks no model:
1. It matches the question to the catalogue by meaning (the same embeddings) and by the names it writes. A query
whose parameter the question names is run from further away (`NAMED`) than one it only resembles (`NEAR`); the
thresholds were measured with `questions.toml`.
2. **The shelves decide whether a question is exact at all.** A query runs only when its exact question is closer
to what was asked than the closest card. A name alone is a weak sign, because the things of the ecosystem share
names: "what is nuclear" writes the name of a tool and of a component, and must get the card of the language,
not the commands of the tool. Measured: before this rule 57 of the 107 open questions of `questions.toml` ran a
query; after it 17 (the ones that name one thing, such as a diagnostic's code or where a kind's file goes), and
none of the exact ones lost its query.
3. The question's own words fill the parameters. A follow-up that names nothing ("describe each of them") takes the
names from the user's earlier messages (`history`).
4. A needed parameter no word gives is not guessed: the query is answered under `needs`.
5. What is left of the question is searched in the shelves as always.

rows.summary: `nuclear-graph knowledge check` fails when a generated file is not what the tree gives now, when a row is invalid, when the manifest is of other rows, when a source of a curated row changed since its review, or when the running graph holds another revision.
body: `nuclear-graph knowledge check` fails when a generated file is not what the tree gives now, when a row is invalid,
when the manifest is of other rows, when a source of a curated row changed since its review, or when the running

rows.summary: `strategy:bug-failing-test`...: 31 of them, on the `playbooks` shelf).
body: **A strategy** is the row of one kind of request a user makes (`strategy:resource-db`, `strategy:refactor-rename`,
`strategy:bug-failing-test`...: 31 of them, on the `playbooks` shelf). What a strategy row says and what a run
does with it is `ADR-developer-0001` of the
[Nuclear Developer](../../../nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/docs/03-adr/0001-a-strategy-for-each-kind-of-request.md).
`POST /v1/strategy` (`nuclear-graph strategy`, MCP `graph_strategy`) says which one a request is, and why:
- An exact sign of the request (`data.signals`: a diagnostic code, a test's output, `rename A to B`, a `GET <url>`
line) outweighs any closeness of meaning.
- Meaning decides between strategies with no exact sign, or the same ones.
- Whether the project has the names the request writes moves the score (`existing`, `new` against the row's
`data.target`).
- A run of the Builder cannot follow a strategy without stages (a question, a command): with `runnable`, such a
strategy comes first only when an exact sign chose it.
- `only` is the strategy a spec names itself (`- Strategy: usecase`).
The answer is at most three strategies, best first, each with the signs that chose it (`why`).

rows.summary: (`Store.near`, `Store.measure`); the store's own index (HNSW) is approximate and is not asked.
body: **The search is exact.** The stored vector of every item a filter matches is compared with the query's
(`Store.near`, `Store.measure`); the store's own index (HNSW) is approximate and is not asked. Once rows were
replaced that index did not reach every item it held: after an ingest 3 cards of 2 617 could not be found, and
which ones changed at every start. A shelf holds hundreds of items, so comparing them all costs milliseconds (173
questions in 42 s, the embedding of each included).
A card is read directly by its id, with a line for each card it links to (`GET /v1/cards/{id}`, `nuclear-graph
card`, MCP `graph_card`).
```sh
nuclear-graph search "como funciona el MCP"                # every shelf
nuclear-graph search "how do I declare an entity" -c platforms -p backend --agents
nuclear-graph card error:N0114                             # one card and what it links to
Limit: keys are exact. A name written with a typo is found by meaning only.

rows.title: The search, and the choice of a strategy — Search
rows.summary: one is brought in and moves up: 0.12 for a word, 0.22 for a longer name or a code.
body: **Search** is by meaning and by exact name at once, over several shelves (`retrieve.nuc`):
- The query is embedded once and each shelf asked answers its closest cards.
- The runs of one to four words of the query are looked up in the cards' `keys` (`$contains`). A card that carries
one is brought in and moves up: 0.12 for a word, 0.22 for a longer name or a code. So `N0114`, `gen resource`,
`usecase` or `mcp` reach their card whatever the rest of the sentence says, in any language.
- A card is also found by the questions its author wrote for it (`asks`).
- Entries are ranked together, each card once. A `docs` row yields to a card (0.04), and a document gives at most
two sections.
- `expand` adds to each card the title and summary of the rows it links to.
- Filters: `agents`, `platform`, and any metadata (`type`, `kind`, `code`).
- A result's `distance` is the closest the card came by meaning, by its text or by any question it answers.

rows with a vector, a document and metadata of texts, numbers, booleans and lists of texts; the filters `$eq $ne
$gt $gte $lt $lte $in $nin $and $or` and, on a list, `$contains`; a query restricted to given ids; lookup by id.
Its full-text filters read the document, which is stored encrypted, so they are of no use here; it has no keyword
index of its own.

rows.title: Security — How it is protected
rows.summary: in constant time, and an allowed request hands its token once.
body: - The server listens on `127.0.0.1` only; a request with an `Origin` header (a web page) is refused.
- Every route but `/v1/health` and the access request needs a token. Tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes, compared
in constant time, and an allowed request hands its token once.
- Documents are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM). The key and the owner token live in the desktop keyring
(`secret-tool`, libsecret), or in `0600` files of the data folder when there is no keyring.
- A graph that starts while its keyring is closed (a service at login) waits for it and never makes a second key or
token.
- The data folder (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/nuclear-graph`, `0700`) is opened only by the server process.
- Only `ingest` writes the shelves of the base: a client writes `memory` and `examples` and cannot plant false
documentation.
- The exact facts are never written to disk: the database is made in memory from the sealed cards, and is
read-only.
- The key of a search engine for the agents (`nuclear-graph web-key brave`) is read from stdin and kept with the
other secrets. The internet tools refuse local addresses.

rows.title: Security — Limits
rows.summary: Protection is per OS user.
body: Protection is per OS user. A program running as you could ask the keyring for the key as the graph does; the graph
stops other users, web pages and programs that only speak HTTP or MCP.

rows.title: Security
rows.summary: Never weaken one of these rules to make something easier: build the access the right way (`connect`, or a request the user allows).
body: Never weaken one of these rules to make something easier: build the access the right way (`connect`, or a request
the user allows).

rows.title: Security — Sensitive data
rows.summary: Sensitive data
body: | Data | Where | How it is protected |
| The text of a card | Chroma, the document | encrypted (AES-256-GCM) |
| The vectors and the metadata (ids, titles, keys) | Chroma | in clear: Chroma searches them. They reveal what a row is about, not its text |
| The documents' key, the owner token, each client's token | the keyring, or `0600` files | per OS user |
| The tokens the server checks | the data folder | SHA-256 hashes |
| The exact facts (names, summaries) | the server's memory | never on disk |

rows.title: Security — Who may read it
rows.summary: Nothing reaches the graph without a token, and no token exists until you allow it.
body: Nothing reaches the graph without a token, and no token exists until you allow it.
| Command | What it does |
| `nuclear-graph connect <client> --scopes read,write` | gives a program access now and keeps its token in your keyring (`--print`: prints the token instead of keeping it) |
| `nuclear-graph requests` | the pending access requests and the allowed clients |
| `nuclear-graph allow <request>` / `deny <request>` | answers a request a program made (`POST /v1/access`) |
| `nuclear-graph revoke <client>` | takes a client's access away (its token stops working at once) |
Scopes: `read` (search, cards, prompts), `write` (remember, add examples), `admin` (ingest, manage: only you, with
the owner token). The two clients of this ecosystem:
```sh
nuclear-graph connect mcp --scopes read,write                 # the MCP server
nuclear-graph connect nuclear-developer --scopes read,write   # the local agents
A program reads its token from `NUCLEAR_GRAPH_TOKEN`, else from the keyring. Without a keyring, `connect` writes
the token to a file of the data folder that only you can read.

rows.title: Update the knowledge base — The procedure
rows.summary: 1. Build.
body: 1. **Build.** `nuclear-graph knowledge build`. It prints the revision, the rows added, changed and removed, the
size of each shelf, and a `review:` line for each curated row whose source changed. With a problem, nothing is
versioned: fix what each line says.
2. **Review.** For each `review:` line, read the change: update the row, or confirm it with
`nuclear-graph knowledge review <id>` when it still holds.
3. **Write what is new and has no structured source**: a capability, a limit, a failure, a procedure. A new tool,
error, kind or version needs nothing: the build reads it.
4. **Add the question the change answers** to `data/questions.toml` (a question with one right answer: a row of
`data/assets/queries/` and its `exact = true` entry).
5. **Check.** `nuclear-graph knowledge check`.
6. **Ingest.** `nuclear-graph ingest`, then `nuclear-graph stats` shows the revision the graph holds.
7. **Ask.** `nuclear-graph knowledge ask` (every question finds its row) and `nuclear-graph knowledge examples`
(every Nuclear example compiles).

rows.title: The Smart Graph
rows.summary: The Nuclear Smart Graph is the library of everything NuclearLang and Synapsis are, kept on your machine.
body: The Nuclear Smart Graph is the library of everything NuclearLang and Synapsis are, kept on your machine. An agent
that writes Nuclear asks it instead of guessing: what a kind means, how a task is done step by step, which tool
does it, what an error means and how it is fixed, what the platform cannot do yet.
- **Private and local.** It runs on `127.0.0.1:7878` for one user of the machine. The cards are encrypted at rest,
every route but the health check needs a token, and no program reads it until you allow that program.
- **Cards, not copied pages.** Each row is a card that answers one question, on the shelf of its kind of question,
linked to the cards it has to do with.
- **Exact when the question has one answer.** "Every tool of the MCP server" gives every tool, the same on every
run: those questions are answered from a database of facts, not by a search by meaning. No model is asked.
Why it exists and what it is not: [the vision](../00-context/vision.md).

rows.summary: The compiler catches the habits of TypeScript, Dart and Python (`N0022`, with an exact `fix`), invented classes (`N0220`) and invented named arguments (`N0219`, it lists the real ones).

- Writing `return`, `;`, `{ }`, `new`, `await`, `const`/`final`/`var`, `&&`, `!x`, `name: value` arguments: use the
sheet's forms (`~x`, `x = 1`, `and`, `not x`, `name = value`).

calls the repository. Another component sees only the `appcomponent`, models, events, guards and screens.

rows.title: NuclearLang
rows.summary: NuclearLang (`.nuc`) is a minimal language transpiled to TypeScript, Dart or Python by declarative dialects.
body: NuclearLang (`.nuc`) is a minimal language transpiled to TypeScript, Dart or Python by declarative dialects. Synapsis
is its framework: three platforms written in Nuclear — `mobile` (dialect `flutter`: the Flutter app is generated in
`build/app`), `backend` (dialects `fastapi` = Python/FastAPI and `nestjs` = TypeScript, built to `build/` by
`nuclear build .`) and `web` (dialect `react` = TypeScript/React). The Nuclear of a platform is the same for every dialect of it; only
the standard library of Nuclear is used on strings, lists and maps (`nuclear help library`), never the target's. Its
syntax is NOT TypeScript, Dart nor Python: read the sheet before writing.
**Make it with the tools.** A product (any software made from Nuclear) is made with the platform's tools:
`nuclear new`, `nuclear gen`, `nuclear make`, the MCP server's tools, `nuclear add` for a library, `nuclear fix`; only
what they leave is written by hand, in Nuclear. Never write target code (`.ts`, `.dart`, `.py`) for a feature, and
never translate React, Node.js, Python or Dart code into Nuclear by hand. Only when strictly necessary, and then say
so: the tool that should have done it is missing something.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — 2. How a model works with it
rows.summary: 1. Inspect.
body: 1. **Inspect.** `project_inspect`: what the project already has, so nothing is declared twice.
2. **Generate.** For every resource the spec names (a model and what is done with it), `generate_resource`. Its
fields come from the API's answer (`from_json`; `api_inspect` shows its shape first), from the spec (`from_spec`)
or from `fields`. When neither gives them, the model looks up the API's documentation (`web_search`, `web_read`)
and, if it is still unclear, asks the user: it never guesses. A use case that only calls a repository method is
`generate_usecase` with `calls`.
3. **The local developer writes the rest.** `developer_task` with what the generators did not write (a use case with
its own rules, a view's details): the local agents plan, write the tests first, write the code, run the tests and
the security review, and answer a journal of everything they did.
4. **Wire.** Each use case the local developer wrote, with `generate_usecase` (its alias in the facade, its route).
5. **Validate.** `nuclear_check` of the project must say `ok` and `nuclear test` must pass.
6. **Correct only what failed**, never what passed. Before writing `.nuc` the model reads `nuclear_brief` and
searches the graph. A run that failed for a passing cause is run again with `developer_retry`.

rows.summary: 7. Review.
body: 7. **Review.** `developer_review` with what was corrected and why: the journal keeps it and the corrected files
become examples the local developer finds next time.
The model writes the code itself only when the local developer is not running, and says so.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — Generators
rows.summary: They write finished code that compiles, never a skeleton to fill in.
body: They write finished code that compiles, never a skeleton to fill in. Each is a `nuclear gen` command:
[the generators' guide](../../../../nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/08-guides/generators.md) has the
options, the examples and what each platform gets.

body: generate_resource(project, "orders", "Order", fields="id:int total:double status:string", source="db")
generate_usecase(project, "orders", "PageOrders", calls="OrderRepository.page", route="GET orders/pages/{page}")
generate_usecase(project, "orders", "CancelOrder", route="POST orders/{id}/cancel")   # CancelOrder is in the project
Nothing is overwritten and nothing is declared twice; `dry_run` shows the files first. A generator that cannot write
something finished refuses and says what to do: `generate_usecase` without `calls`, for a use case the project does
not declare, answers where to write it.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — Generators
rows.summary: Generators
body: | Tool | What it does |
| `project_inspect(project)` | the project's platform and dialect, its components with their declarations by kind, the generators of its platform |
| `generate_component(project, component)` | a new component with its facade |

| `generate_resource(project, component, name, from_json \| from_spec \| fields, source, path, actions, screen, plural, dry_run)` | a resource: models, repository, a use case per action, the facade's aliases, the controller (backend) or a screen with its state manager (mobile, web), the tests |

| `generate_usecase(project, component, name, calls, route, dry_run)` | a use case wired into its component: its alias in the facade and, with `route` (backend), its route. With `calls` the use case is written too, because it only calls that repository method; without it the use case is one the project already has |
| `generate_screen(project, component, screen, route)` | mobile and web: a screen with its state manager and state model, for a view that is not a resource's list |
| `api_inspect(url, project, component, name)` | the shape of a public API's JSON answer; with a project, the files `generate_resource` would write from it |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — The compiler and the command line
rows.summary: The compiler and the command line
body: | Tool | What it does |
| `nuclear_check(code \| path, dialect)` | `ok`, or one line per error with its fix, for a piece of Nuclear or a whole project |
| `nuclear_build(code, dialect)` | what a piece of Nuclear becomes in the dialect's language |
| `nuclear_fmt(code)` | the piece in the canonical layout |
| `nuclear_help(word, dialect)` | the documentation of a kind, a decorator, a topic or a command |
| `nuclear_brief(dialect)` | the short sheet of Nuclear and a platform: read before writing `.nuc` |

| `nuclear_defs(name, dialect, project?)` | a declaration of the type definitions (a class or `Class.member` of a library); with the project's folder, also of a package the project added (`nuclear_project` with `add`) |

| `nuclear_project(project, command, args)` | `new`, `build`, `install`, `test`, `check`, `analyze`, `make`, `gen`, `migrate`, `add`, `remove`, `explain` in a project (`add` with a name: a package of the target and its type definitions) |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — The internet
rows.summary: The internet
body: | Tool | What it does |

| `web_search(query, pages)` | searches the internet and answers the first results with the text of their pages (your own SearXNG with `NUCLEAR_SEARXNG_URL`, Brave with `nuclear-graph web-key brave`, else Wikipedia) |
| `web_read(url)` | the text of a public page, without its code blocks. Local addresses are refused |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — The local developer
rows.summary: The local developer
body: | Tool | What it does |

| `developer_task(project, title, description, criteria, use_case)` | **the first step of every task that writes `.nuc`**: the local agents do the whole task in the project (plan, tests first, code, verification, security, artifacts) and answer the run's journal. `use_case`: `feature`, `bug`, `refactor`, `test` |

| `developer_retry(project, run, from_stage, from_step, scratch)` | a run again: from the step that failed, every step that passed kept; the whole of `from_stage`; from one step (`from_step`: its id in the journal, passed or failed) and every step after it; or from scratch (`scratch`: every stage again). What the steps left out wrote is undone first |
| `developer_review(project, run, notes, files)` | **the last step**: the lead's corrections, kept in the journal; each corrected file goes to the graph's examples |
| `developer_code(task, platform, path, kind, context, project)` | one `.nuc` file outside a task, written, checked and repaired by the local model. It returns the file; it does not write it |
| `developer_test(task, code, platform)` | the Nuclear tests of a piece of code |
| `developer_security(code, platform)` | the security findings of a piece of code |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — The Smart Graph
rows.summary: The Smart Graph
body: | Tool | What it does |

| `graph_strategy(request, platform)` | **the first call for any request**: which kind of request it is (a whole system, a component, one screen, a use case, a rename, a failing test, a question...), the signs that say so, and the plan of that kind, step by step with the tool of each step |

| `graph_answer(question, platform)` | the exact answer of a question that has one (every command of a tool, the tools of this server and their parameters, the commands that write a kind, a diagnostic by its code, the stages of the Builder, a version...): the rows of the graph's database, whole, never recalled; then the cards the shelves answer by meaning. For "which", "list", "what are the" questions |

| `graph_search(query, shelf, k, platform, kind, type)` | the cards that answer a question, by meaning and by exact name (a diagnostic code, a command, a kind), each with the rows it links to. `shelf`: `concepts`, `language`, `platforms`, `tools`, `errors`, `capabilities`, `playbooks`, `examples`, `docs`, `memory`; empty searches all |
| `graph_card(id)` | one row by its id: `error:N0114`, `kind:backend.usecase`, `tool:nuclear.gen.usecase`, `mcp:generate_usecase`, `playbook:add-a-use-case` |
| `graph_prompt(use_case)` | the validated prompt of `feature`, `refactor`, `bug`, `docs`, `diagram`, `test`, `security`, `piece`, `plan` |

rows.summary: The Smart Graph
rows.body: | `graph_remember(id, text, collection, project)` | keeps a decision (`memory`) or a solved example (`examples`) for the local developer and later sessions |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — 4. When a tool fails
rows.summary: The graph knows every tool of this page: ask it with `graph_card("mcp:<tool>")`, or ask the editor's chat (`Ctrl+Alt+A`) in your own words.
body: | The tool answers | What to do |

| `the local developer is not running at ...` | `nuclear-builder setup --status` says what is missing; restart it in *Settings and integrations*, or with [the command of your system](../../../../installer/docs/08-guides/ai-setup.md#5-after-the-set-up) |
| the graph refuses the client | `nuclear-graph connect mcp --scopes read,write`, with the graph running |
| `... is not inside a Synapsis project (no config.nuc)` | give the project's folder: `nuclear new <name>` creates one |
| `'<command>' is not allowed here` | the `nuclear_project` tool runs only the commands of its list |
| a generator refuses | its message says what is missing: [when a generator refuses](../../../../nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/08-guides/generators.md#4-when-a-generator-refuses) |
The graph knows every tool of this page: ask it with `graph_card("mcp:<tool>")`, or ask the editor's chat
(`Ctrl+Alt+A`) in your own words.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang
rows.summary: MCP is the Model Context Protocol: an AI client (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) starts a program and calls the tools it offers.
body: MCP is the **Model Context Protocol**: an AI client (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) starts a program and calls
the tools it offers. `nuclear-mcp` is that program for NuclearLang. It speaks MCP over stdio and gives a
frontier model four things: the **generators** that write the standard code, the **local developer** that writes what
is left, the **Smart Graph** to look things up instead of guessing, and the **compiler** to check everything.
The server also tells the model how to work, so every client behaves the same: generate first, let the local
developer write the rest, then validate and correct.
